title: LetsPlayPro — Backend Services
description: Request rate, error rate, latency, and resource usage across all seven services, plus infra pod health. Import this directly (Dashboards -> New -> Import -> Upload JSON) once the k8s-monitoring chart has been running for a few minutes.

panels.title: Request rate by service
panels.description: req/s, summed across all pods of each service — a sudden drop usually means the service is down or unreachable (from the gateway's own request rate dropping while others hold steady), not that traffic genuinely stopped.

panels.title: Error rate (5xx) by service
panels.description: Percentage of requests returning 5xx. Distinct from 4xx (client errors — expected background noise from bad input, invalid tokens, etc.) — this panel deliberately only counts server-side failures.

panels.title: p50 / p95 / p99 latency by service
panels.description: The gap between p50 and p99 matters more than either number alone — a service where most requests are fast but a real minority are very slow (a wide gap) has a different problem than one that's uniformly a bit slow (a narrow gap), even if their averages look identical.

panels.title: Memory (RSS) by service
panels.description: Resident memory per pod. A steady upward slope with no plateau across multiple deploys is the classic memory-leak shape — worth a closer look before it hits the pod's memory limit and gets OOMKilled (see the restart panel below).

panels.title: CPU usage by service
panels.description: Cores used, not percent of a single core — 1.0 means fully saturating one core. Compare against each Deployment's resources.limits.cpu in k8s/apps/*.yaml to see how close to throttling a service is running.

panels.title: Event loop lag by service
panels.description: Node-specific canary metric — how long the event loop is delayed processing the next tick. Rising lag means something synchronous/blocking is running on the main thread (a large JSON.parse, an unindexed Mongo query resolving synchronously-ish under load, bcrypt hashing) and every OTHER request on that pod is queued behind it, not just the slow one.

panels.title: Pod restarts (all pods, letsplaypro namespace)
panels.description: Covers mongo-*/redis/rabbitmq too, not just the app services — these come from kube-state-metrics (clusterMetrics.enabled in the Helm values), not from anything the app services expose themselves. A climbing counter for any pod is worth investigating even if nothing else here looks wrong yet.

panels.title: Pods not Ready (letsplaypro namespace)
panels.description: Anything above zero for more than a minute or two (past normal rollout time) means a pod is failing its readinessProbe — check whether it's still connecting to a dependency (Mongo/RabbitMQ/Redis) or genuinely stuck.

panels.title: Messages processed by outcome
panels.description: 'failure' climbing without 'success' also climbing means the RabbitMQ queue is backing up — check this alongside the RabbitMQ management UI (or its own queue-depth metrics, not yet wired up here — see backend README's observability notes) for actual queue depth.

panels.title: Message processing time (p95)
panels.description: Mostly reflects SMTP send latency — a sustained jump here usually means the SMTP provider is slow, not this service.
